To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the national performing arts companies have increased ticket prices, but have not increased audiences or the amount of performing they do.
the subsidized performing arts companies have been able to increase ticket prices significantly, and to exploit consumer surplus and willingness to pay, without significantly increasing their output.

(1) the subsidized performing arts in Britain have been successful in exploiting the consumer surplus in the demand for their products, but (2) this has not been achieved by attracting more people to their performances or by increasing the number of performances staged, but instead by increasing ticket prices and thus the average ticket price, and (3) this has been achieved by a combination of increases in the price of tickets, reductions in the price of concessions and reductions in the number of concessions available.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the economics of the national arts companies in Britain.
the economics of the national grant- aid companies and the extent to which their economic and financial performance is consistent with the objectives of cultural policy.
the economic performance of the national performing companies, and the implications of this for the future funding and management of the national performing art companies.

, despite the significant increases in box office revenue and the exploitation of audience willingness-to-pay achieved over this period, these major companies have not generally increased their audiences or the output of performances and productions.
the national performing arts companies are not exploiting their audiences, nor the potential of their audiences to increase their attendance at their productions.

the national performing arts companies, with the exception of Opera North and the Royal Shakespeare Company, have been successful in exploiting their audiences' willingness-to-pay, in raising box office income to fund increased administration and staffing costs, but have not significantly increased their output in terms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

there has been a general decline in the number of performances, productions and attendances by the national subsidized companies, and an increase in their administrative, staffing and other overheads, which has been financed by increases in box office receipts and government grants, and that these increases have been achieved by exploiting consumer surplus and audience willingness-to-pay.

we found that the national performing arts companies have been successful at exploiting the willingness-to-pay of their audiences, but that this has been at the expense of the consumer surplus that they might have been expected to generate.
we have shown how the economics of the subsidized national performing arts have been transformed over a ten-year period, and have identified the reasons for this.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the national performing arts companies have achieved a significant increase in box office revenue, but this has not been matched by an increase in the number of people attending these performances, and has not been sufficient to offset reductions in subsidy.
the national performing arts companies have been successful over the last decade in exploiting audience willingness to pay and increasing ticket prices.
the economic performance of the subsidized national performing arts in England has been poor.
